title: How much does it cost to get fit? A realistic UK budget
summary: Memberships, food, equipment and support: understand the whole budget before you spend.
bodyHtml:
You can start getting fitter without buying a subscription, a smartwatch or a cupboard full of powders. Walking where it is safe and accessible, using suitable exercises at home and making practical changes to meals you already eat can all form part of a routine. The NHS exercise hub provides exercise guidance and resources you can read without paying.

That does not mean every person can exercise comfortably for free. You might need suitable footwear, an accessible venue, childcare or someone to help you get started. A useful budget starts with your circumstances, rather than a shopping list supplied by the fitness industry.

Separate starting costs from ongoing costs

Make two short lists. The first is what you genuinely need before your first session. The second is what will leave your bank account repeatedly. Check what you already own before buying either. A perfectly serviceable T-shirt does not become unsuitable because you have decided to exercise in it.

Type of costExamplesQuestion to ask
One-offSuitable shoes, basic equipment, introductory tuitionDo I need this now, and could I borrow or use what I have?
RecurringMembership, app, coachingWhat practical help will I use each week?
IndirectParking, travel, childcareDoes the routine still fit my budget after these are included?
OptionalSupplements, branded clothing, upgraded tracking devicesWhat problem would this solve that my current setup cannot?

Three illustrative budgets

The figures below are invented planning examples, not quoted gym prices or UK averages. They show how to calculate your own budget. Food is excluded because everyone already has a food budget and changes need comparing separately.

ExampleCalculationFirst-year total
Home routine using existing clothing£30 one-off equipment allowance; free guidance£30
Local gym routine£30 membership × 12, plus £10 travel × 12, plus £20 joining fee£500
Gym with weekly personal trainingThe £500 above, plus 48 sessions at an illustrative £40£2,420

The third route is not automatically better. It pays for more individual time. Someone who needs instruction and scheduled appointments may value that. Someone who already knows how to train may gain very little from the additional expense. Equally, a home setup is poor value if you cannot find suitable space to use it.

Where does NUFI fit?

NUFI’s confirmed listed prices are £29.99 per month or one £99 annual payment, equivalent to £8.25 per month. Twelve monthly payments total £359.88. These are different payment options, so compare both before deciding.

NUFI is designed to bring programmes, meal planning, tracking and AI guidance together. Supplements and flavour shots are optional, separately priced products. Do not include them in a minimum membership budget. The current site is a preview: account access and payment are not connected, and final membership terms need to be available before you buy. A displayed AI coach should not be mistaken for a dedicated human trainer.

Your food bill does not have to become a second membership

Work from what you currently buy. If you replace an existing lunch with another lunch, the relevant figure is the difference in cost, not the entire price of the new meal. Buying an extra protein snack alongside everything you already eat is additional spending. Replacing a more expensive convenience snack might be a saving.

Start by recording one ordinary week of food spending, including top-up shops and lunches outside the home. Then choose two or three changes you would actually enjoy. Avoid claiming a saving until you have compared like-for-like portions and included ingredients bought specifically for the new recipes.

Spend where the routine breaks down

If the obstacle is knowing what to do, a suitable programme may help. If it is technique or confidence, some individual instruction could be more useful. If it is deciding what everyone will eat, a manageable meal plan may deserve attention before more exercise equipment.

Give yourself a spending limit that leaves normal bills comfortable. Look at the routine after a few weeks: what did you use, what helped, and what was unnecessary? Keep the parts earning their place.

Before comparing products, finish this sentence: “The thing I need help with each week is…” You can then browse the programme options or the recipes with a clear reason for being there.
shortAnswer: Getting fitter can start with no new subscription at all. Your realistic budget depends on the help, equipment and facilities you need, plus any extra travel or childcare. NUFI’s listed prices are £29.99 monthly or £99 paid annually, but neither supplements nor a gym membership are prerequisites for beginning. Compare total spending over a year and pay to solve a specific obstacle.

title: How much does a personal trainer cost in the UK?
summary: Compare session prices, packages and the support included in the fee.
bodyHtml:
As a useful starting point, PureGym’s published benchmark, checked on 15 September 2026, is £30–£65 for a 45–60-minute personal-training session outside London. Its London benchmark is £45–£65. Trainers set their own rates, so these are one provider’s broad guide, not a nationwide tariff or a ceiling on what a specialist can charge.

The number that matters is your written quote for the service you want. A £40 session and a £60 session cannot be compared fairly until you know the duration, what happens between appointments and whether the trainer is a good fit for you.

What does that mean over a month or year?

FrequencyAt £30 a sessionAt £65 a session
Four sessions£120£260
Eight sessions£240£520
48 sessions across a year£1,440£3,120

These are calculations from the quoted range, not package offers. Four sessions are not automatically a calendar month: some months contain five of your usual training day. The annual example allows 48 appointments, rather than assuming you train every week without a holiday or interruption.

PureGym says personal-training fees are separate from its gym membership. Elsewhere, studio access might be included or charged separately. Add travel and any childcare to your own total. Ask whether the quoted price is the full consumer amount, including any applicable VAT, before paying.

What are you buying beyond an hour in the gym?

A useful trainer should be able to explain the purpose of your plan, help you understand the exercises and change the work when your ability or circumstances change. That can involve preparation outside your appointment. But do not assume every fee includes unlimited messaging, nutrition support or a programme for the other days.

Ask what happens during an ordinary week. If you train alone twice between appointments, will you know which exercises to do? If the equipment is occupied, will you have alternatives? If you miss a week through work, how will you restart? The answers reveal more than a promise to help you “transform”.

Questions worth asking before buying a block

  • How long is each session, including any warm-up and discussion?
  • What relevant qualifications and experience do you have with people starting where I am?
  • Will I work with you consistently, or with different trainers?
  • Is a programme for independent sessions included?
  • What contact is included between appointments, and when should I expect replies?
  • What are the notice, rescheduling, expiry and refund conditions?
  • Can we agree how to judge whether the arrangement is helping after the first few weeks?

You should be comfortable asking those questions. You are choosing a professional service, not auditioning to be sufficiently motivated.

When can fewer sessions be better value?

Suppose your main concern is using equipment confidently. An introductory block that teaches you how to follow a manageable routine may suit you better than an open-ended weekly commitment. Agree that purpose in advance: ask what you should understand and be able to practise by the end.

Someone else might know the exercises but need an appointment they can keep and a person who notices when the plan no longer fits. Regular sessions may be worth more to them. Frequency should follow the problem you want help with, rather than the package the trainer happens to sell.

Shared sessions can reduce the amount each person pays, where a trainer offers them. Check that the group is small enough and the training appropriate for everyone. Lower individual attention is part of the trade-off.

When an app is not a fair substitute

An app may help organise training and meals, but it does not put a trainer beside you. If you want live observation, immediate feedback or reassurance in an unfamiliar gym, compare options that actually provide those things. A low app price does not remove that difference.

For ongoing pain, rehabilitation or a medical condition affecting exercise, seek a suitably qualified healthcare professional’s advice about the support you need. A general trainer or app should not promise to diagnose the problem.

Make the first conversation specific

Try: “I have two evenings available, I am new to strength training, and I want to feel confident exercising on my own. What would you suggest, what would it cost in total, and how would we review it?”

If your needs are mainly choosing and organising sessions, browse the programme options first. If they involve a person watching and helping you practise, speak to a trainer about that directly. Buy the kind of support you need, with a price and plan you understand.
shortAnswer: PureGym publishes a rough benchmark of £30–£65 for a 45–60-minute personal-training session outside London, with trainers setting their own fees. At that range, four sessions cost £120–£260 before any gym membership. Your quote should specify session length, frequency, between-session support and package conditions. Paying more only makes sense when the extra service addresses something you need.

title: How much does online fitness coaching cost, and what should you get for your money?
summary: Understand the difference between a workout plan, regular check-ins and individual coaching.
bodyHtml:
There is no single useful price for “online fitness coaching” because the label can mean app access, group support or a personal coach reviewing your progress. The biggest question is how much individual attention you are buying and what that person actually does.

Two published UK examples, checked on 15 September 2026, illustrate the difference. Team RH lists £8.99 monthly payments or £79.99 paid annually; its terms specify a 12-month minimum commitment. DH Kettlebells lists an online coaching package at £150 per month, describing individual programming, weekly check-ins and video technique feedback. These services have different formats and specialisms. Neither price establishes a UK average.

Start with the service, then compare the fee

FormatWhat to establishMay suit you when
App or programme accessWhich plans are available and how you select an appropriate oneYou can exercise independently and want structure
App with shared supportWho replies, whether they know your history and what changes they can makeYou want help with general questions and regular encouragement
Individual online coachingWho reviews your week, how often and what feedback you receiveYour circumstances need individual adjustments
Live remote sessionsHow many appointments you receive, their length and how observation worksYou want scheduled, real-time instruction at home

An app with a chat button is not automatically individual coaching. A coach delivering a plan through an app may provide considerable individual care. The delivery method alone tells you little; the working arrangement tells you much more.

Turn the headline price into the full commitment

At £8.99 a month, twelve Team RH instalments total £107.88. Paying monthly does not make that particular offer a cancel-any-time monthly contract. Its £79.99 upfront annual option is a different payment basis. This is exactly why you should read the contract alongside the price.

For an invented comparison, a £150 monthly service used for six months totals £900 before any extra costs. If there were a separate £50 setup fee, the total would be £950. That setup fee is illustrative, not a claim about DH Kettlebells. Ask every provider about setup charges, equipment, gym access and any minimum term.

Request the full price including any applicable VAT. “From” prices and first-month discounts can be useful starting information, but they do not answer what your particular arrangement will cost.

What should individual coaching look like?

Ask a prospective coach to describe a week when your plan goes wrong. You had two late shifts, could not get to the gym and found one exercise uncomfortable. Who reads that update? What information do they need? What will they change? When will you hear back?

A specific answer might explain a check-in process, how exercise substitutions are agreed and the limits of remote observation. It should also explain when pain or another concern needs a healthcare professional. A vague assurance that they are “always there” leaves the practical arrangement unclear.

Find out whether the person whose videos persuaded you to enquire will coach you. If another team member provides the service, you should know that before paying. Also ask how holidays and staff changes are handled.

When a cheaper option is sufficient

You may not need individual coaching if you already exercise confidently and simply want a programme you can follow. Paying for frequent check-ins will not add much if you do not want to provide updates or discuss your routine.

Conversely, if each week has different shifts, equipment or limitations, a generic plan may leave the main problem unresolved. A higher fee can be sensible when it buys relevant attention you will actually use. It is not sensible merely because expensive feels more serious.

How to compare NUFI honestly

NUFI is designed as a programme and meal-planning system with tracking and AI guidance. Its listed prices are £29.99 monthly or £99 in one annual payment. Twelve monthly payments are £359.88; £99 annually is equivalent to £8.25 per month. Dedicated human coaching hours are not confirmed as part of those prices.

The current site is a preview and account access and payments are not connected. Evaluate the intended approach, but ask to see the working service and final terms before purchasing. Compare AI support with AI support and individual human attention with individual human attention.

Write down the two things you most need a provider to do each week. Then ask each provider how its service handles those exact needs. If you cannot explain what the additional fee buys you, keep asking before committing.
shortAnswer: Online coaching covers very different services. Current examples range from Team RH’s £8.99 monthly instalments on a 12-month contract to DH Kettlebells’ £150 monthly individual online coaching package. These are examples, not a UK market average. Compare human contact, programme changes, feedback and the minimum commitment before deciding whether a fee represents good value for you.

title: How much should you pay for a fitness app?
summary: Look at what you will use, subscription terms and the total annual cost.
bodyHtml:
A fitness app is worth paying for when it makes something useful easier to do repeatedly. That might be choosing a suitable workout, planning meals or keeping a record of progress. There is no sensible rule that everyone should spend a particular amount.

Start by asking whether you need a paid app at all. Nike’s official Training Club listing offers free access to workouts for Nike members. If guided workouts are the only missing piece in your routine, try an appropriate free option before adding another subscription.

What published prices look like

Prices checked on 15 September 2026. These examples have different features and availability; this is a cost comparison, not a claim of equivalent service.

OptionMonthly priceAnnual paymentTwelve monthly payments
Nike Training ClubFree workout accessNo workout subscription fee listed£0
The Body Coach£14.99£89.99 standard annual price£179.88
NUFI£29.99£99£359.88

The Body Coach also advertises occasional offers; check the price, eligibility and renewal amount shown when you subscribe. We have used its standard checkout prices here so an offer does not quietly become a permanent comparison.

NUFI’s annual price is one £99 payment, equivalent to £8.25 per month. The current website is a preview: payment and account access are not connected. Its intended programme, meal-planning, tracking and AI support features need to be assessed in the working service before purchase.

A year is not always the right first purchase

An annual option can have a lower total price while requiring more money today. A monthly equivalent such as £8.25 is arithmetic, not permission to pay that amount each month. Check the actual payment schedule, minimum term, renewal arrangements and cancellation process.

Do not buy twelve months simply to prove you are committed. If you are uncertain about the format, look for a demonstration or a clearly described trial where offered. Test the task you need most, rather than scrolling through an attractive library for ten minutes.

Try an ordinary Tuesday

Before comparing feature lists, imagine using the app on a normal, slightly inconvenient day. You have twenty minutes, a busy household and limited equipment. Can you find an appropriate session quickly? Are the instructions understandable? Can you tell how that session fits into a programme?

For meal planning, try a week that includes leftovers, a meal out and somebody who will not touch mushrooms. Check how easily the plan can be changed, whether the recipes suit your budget and what shopping-list functionality actually works. A long recipe count is less useful than five meals your household will eat.

What extra features deserve extra money?

  • Clear progression, if you want help deciding what to do next.
  • Meal-planning tools, if choosing and organising food is a recurring struggle.
  • Accessible instructions and exercise alternatives that suit your circumstances.
  • Useful tracking that does not demand more administration than you want.
  • Defined support, where you understand whether replies come from AI, a shared team or a dedicated person.

A feature earns its place when it reduces a difficulty you have. It does not earn it because the comparison chart contains a tick.

Check the costs outside the app

Some workouts need equipment or a gym. Some recipes involve ingredients you would not usually buy. Wearable integrations may be irrelevant unless you already own the device. These costs belong in the comparison if they are needed for the way you intend to use the service.

NUFI supplements and flavour shots are optional products, separately charged. An app should not leave you thinking its food guidance is unusable without buying the brand’s products.

Choose for use, then review

Set a modest test: two planned training sessions and one useful meal-planning session a week, for example. This is a usage check, not a prescribed exercise target. Ask whether the app helped and what still got in the way.

If a free option does enough, keep it. If one paid tool replaces several tasks you struggle with, examine it more closely. Browse programmes and recipes, then decide which part you would use next Tuesday. That answer is more valuable than choosing the app with the longest feature list.
shortAnswer: Pay for the help you expect to use regularly, after checking whether a free option covers it. Nike Training Club offers free workout access; The Body Coach lists £14.99 monthly or £89.99 annually at standard pricing; NUFI lists £29.99 monthly or £99 annually. Compare full-year cost, actual features and contract terms rather than the number of workouts advertised.

title: Is healthy eating really more expensive? Comparing a week of everyday meals
summary: A fair comparison of ordinary meals, portion sizes and the weekly food shop.
bodyHtml:
Eating more healthily can cost less, the same or more than your current routine. Anyone promising that it will always be cheaper is ignoring how different people’s circumstances are. A household already buying the least expensive food has less room to cut costs than one regularly buying lunches and takeaways.

The useful question is: “Can I improve the meals we already eat within the money and time we have?” The answer does not start with replacing everything in the kitchen with products wearing the word “wellness”.

Healthy does not mean premium

The NHS Eatwell Guide includes ordinary starchy foods, vegetables, fruit, protein foods and dairy or alternatives. Fruit and vegetables can be fresh, frozen or tinned. Beans and lentils are among the protein options. None of this requires a special food brand.

That leaves plenty of scope for familiar meals: a jacket potato with beans, a vegetable omelette with bread, or a curry built around pulses. The full recipe and the overall pattern matter. A single ingredient or a low price does not tell you everything about a meal.

A seven-day dinner comparison

This is an illustrative planning exercise for two adults eating seven dinners. Every price below is an invented, rounded ingredient-cost allowance, not a supermarket quote or an observed household saving. Portions, recipes and nutritional content are not identical. Breakfasts, lunches, snacks, drinks, cooking energy and delivery are excluded.

FridayFish, peas and potatoes£5Same meal£5

SundayVegetable and bean chilli with rice£4Same meal£4
TotalFourteen adult dinners£30Fourteen adult dinners£26

The £4 difference belongs to the example, not a promise about your shop. The point is that a few practical substitutions may be enough; you do not have to reinvent all seven dinners. Menu A is not labelled “bad”, and menu B is not a complete prescribed diet.

What actual ingredient prices can tell us

As a checked example on 15 September 2026, Tesco listed 500g of East End dried lentils at £1.50 and 650g of chicken breast at £4.90. Using 200g of those lentils costs 60p; using 300g of that chicken costs about £2.26. These are ingredient costs at regular listed prices, excluding delivery.

They do not make complete, nutritionally identical meals. You still need to account for vegetables, starches, sauce and other ingredients, and the whole pack is what you pay for at the till. Use the calculation to explore a recipe you enjoy, rather than to declare one food universally better.

Compare the till receipt and the food you use

A recipe may use 10p of spice but require you to buy a whole jar. That makes the first shop more expensive than its portion-cost calculation. Conversely, a bag of rice bought this week may feed you again next week. Keep pack spending and ingredient-use costs separate.

Include the top-up trips, purchased lunches and food left uneaten. A slightly dearer bag of frozen vegetables may fit your household better than fresh vegetables you cannot finish. Convenience has a legitimate place when cooking time or energy is limited.

What makes a plan unrealistic?

Bulk buying assumes you have spare cash and storage. Batch cooking assumes you have equipment, time and somewhere to keep meals safely. A meal plan that needs a different shop for every bargain may save money on paper and cost you an afternoon.

Food allergies, medical dietary needs and sensory preferences can narrow your choices. Work with those needs rather than treating them as a failure to budget. If food access itself is the problem, buying a subscription is not the first solution.

Try a smaller change this week

Choose three familiar dinners. See whether one can use more pulses, one can use vegetables already in the freezer, and one can deliberately use leftovers or ingredients from another meal. Price the actual packs at your shop, then decide what fits.

Browse the recipes for ideas, but keep your household’s preferences in charge. A useful meal-planning service should help you organise food you can afford and enjoy. It should not make ordinary shopping feel inadequate.
shortAnswer: Healthy eating does not automatically require a bigger food budget, but it can cost more depending on your starting point, dietary needs and access to shops or cooking facilities. Compare complete meals and what you actually spend across a week. Ordinary beans, lentils, frozen vegetables and familiar staples can help; premium “health” products are not a requirement.

title: How much does a high-protein diet cost? A realistic weekly shopping list
summary: See how everyday protein sources fit into a realistic shopping budget.
bodyHtml:
You do not need a daily steak, a protein bar subscription or a second fridge to include protein regularly. A sample basket of everyday protein foods below costs £14.72 at the listed prices checked on 15 September 2026. It is one adult’s example shopping list for planning a week, with some stock potentially carried forward. It is not a complete food shop or a prescribed diet.

“High protein” is not a single meal plan with a single price. Your needs, appetite, dietary choices and the rest of your food affect what makes sense. Buying the largest possible amount of protein is not the goal. Building meals you can afford and keep eating is more useful.

A protein-staples shopping list

These are Tesco UK online regular listed prices, excluding delivery, with no Clubcard discount used. Local availability, pack labels and prices can change.

FoodBuyCost
Chicken breast filletsTwo 650g packs£9.80
East End red split lentilsOne 500g dry pack£1.50
Chickpeas in waterTwo 400g tins, each 240g drained£0.82
Growers Harvest kidney beansTwo 400g tins, each 240g drained£0.70
Creamfields fat-free Greek-style yogurtTwo 500g pots£1.90
TotalProtein staples only£14.72

You do not have to buy this exact basket. Replace chicken with foods suitable for your preferences and needs; replace dairy appropriately if you cannot eat it. Recalculate the actual products, because alternatives do not necessarily have the same price or protein content.

What else belongs in the budget?

Protein is one part of eating well. The NHS balanced-diet guidance includes a variety of food groups. A shopping list consisting only of the table above would leave important parts of everyday meals missing.

For a budgeting exercise, you might add £6 for oats, bread, rice or potatoes, £12 for fruit and vegetables, £5 for milk or an appropriate alternative and other foods, and £3 for oil and flavouring ingredients. Those £26 allowances are invented planning figures, not a second verified basket. Adding them to £14.72 gives £40.72 as an illustrative one-person food budget to test against your actual shop. It is not a guaranteed complete or nutritionally assessed weekly menu.

Your first week may cost more if cupboards are empty; later weeks may use remaining rice, lentils or seasonings. Larger appetites, dietary restrictions and more costly local shops also change the total. Do not make meals inadequate to force them into an example budget.

How could those staples become meals?

DayExample dinnerPlanning advantage
MondayChicken, rice and vegetablesUse familiar ingredients
TuesdayLentil and vegetable curryCook additional portions if storage allows
WednesdayChicken and chickpea wrapsUse some of the same vegetables
ThursdayBean chilli with riceUse remaining opened pulses promptly
FridayChicken with potatoes and peasUse frozen vegetables as needed
SaturdayLentil and tomato pastaReuse cupboard ingredients
SundayChicken and vegetable tray bakePlan around what remains

These are ideas, not full recipes, quantities or a complete diet. Add breakfasts, lunches and enough food for your appetite. Yogurt can be part of breakfast with oats and fruit; pulses can go into lunches. If you prefer more variety, substitute fish, eggs, tofu or other foods and update the budget. You are allowed to get bored with chicken.

Buy for the week you have

Plan how you will use or freeze fresh food before its use-by date. Do not assume a pack purchased at the start of the week will remain suitable until Sunday. Follow its label and the Food Standards Agency’s storage guidance. Freeze suitable portions promptly if the schedule calls for them later.

If you have little storage or time, smaller packs and ready-to-use options may be the realistic choice even when their unit price is higher. A bargain you cannot safely store or finish is not much of a bargain.

Do you need protein powder as well?

There is no automatic reason to add it because you have started exercising. First look at the foods you already eat and what you need help with. A powder may be convenient for some people, but the label, price, tolerance and purpose should justify it.

NUFI’s intended meal-planning approach should work with ordinary groceries. Its supplements are optional, separately priced products. Start with a week of meals from the recipe section that you would enjoy, then build your actual shopping list. The useful result is a manageable food routine, not the most impressive protein receipt.

The most useful budget combines foods you enjoy with realistic pack sizes, variety and minimal waste.

title: What are the cheapest protein sources? Comparing the cost per 25g of protein
summary: Compare food on the same basis, including pack sizes and the amount you actually eat.
bodyHtml:
In the five ordinary foods checked here, dried lentils give the lowest ingredient cost per 25g of protein. That does not prove they are the cheapest product in every UK shop, or that you should eat enough lentils alone to supply that amount at each meal. It gives you a fairer way to compare the products in front of you.

Pack price alone can mislead. A large tub may cost more at the till but less for the amount you use. A product with “protein” on the front may contain less protein per pound spent than an ordinary food beside it. The useful numbers are on the label.

The calculation

First find the protein in the whole edible pack: edible pack weight in grams, divided by 100, multiplied by the label’s protein per 100g. Then divide the pack price by that total protein and multiply by 25.

For example, a 500g pack containing 23.8g protein per 100g has 119g protein across the pack. If it costs £1.50, the calculation is £1.50 ÷ 119 × 25 = about 32p per 25g of protein. This is ingredient arithmetic using the label, not a laboratory test or an instruction to eat a specific portion.

Five checked UK examples

Tesco UK online regular listed prices and nutrition information, checked 15 September 2026; delivery and cooking energy excluded. We have not applied loyalty discounts. Costs are rounded to the nearest penny.

Food and packPack priceProtein per 100gCost per 25g protein
East End lentils, 500g dry£1.5023.8g, uncooked£0.32
Growers Harvest kidney beans, 240g drained£0.357.9g, drained£0.46
Tesco chickpeas, 240g drained£0.417.8g, drained£0.55
Creamfields Greek-style yogurt, 500g£0.956.4g, as sold£0.74
Tesco chicken breast, 650g raw£4.9021.5g, raw£0.88

The two tins are sold as 400g including liquid; the calculations use 240g drained food. The label basis matters. We used a lentil product with clearly stated uncooked nutrition because combining a dry pack weight with cooked-food nutrition would give a misleading result.

The portion-size catch

To supply 25g protein from one food alone would take approximately 105g dry lentils, 316g drained kidney beans, 321g drained chickpeas, 391g of this yogurt or 116g raw chicken, using the labels above. Those weights are mathematical comparisons, not serving recommendations.

In practice, you might eat a smaller amount of lentils with rice, or yogurt with oats, and obtain protein from several parts of the meal. You do not have to make every ingredient reach the comparison amount by itself. The cheapest number can become a very large bowl when a food is less protein-dense.

Do not mix raw and cooked numbers

Cooking changes the amount of water in food. Dry lentils absorb water; meat commonly loses water. That changes protein per 100g even when you have not bought additional food. Match the weight you are using to the state specified on the label.

For foods with bones, shells or liquid you discard, use the edible portion where reliable information is available. Do not count the full weight as edible protein. When the information is unclear, choose a product with a clearer label or keep the result approximate rather than manufacturing precision.

What this table cannot tell you

It does not measure whether a food tastes good to you, whether you tolerate it, or whether the whole meal meets your needs. It does not assess every vitamin, mineral or aspect of protein quality. A balanced eating pattern involves variety across food groups. Optimising a single nutrient at the expense of everything else is not the purpose.

Preparation also matters. Dried pulses need cooking according to their instructions. Ready-to-use tins cost differently but may suit a rushed evening. If a slightly more expensive ingredient helps you make a meal you enjoy, it can still be good value.

Use the same method for powders

For an invented example, a 1kg powder priced at £20 and labelled 75g protein per 100g contains 750g protein. Its cost per 25g is about 67p, before delivery or anything mixed into it. That example is not a current product quote and does not prove a powder is needed.

Include any delivery charge, check allergens and do not treat a serving of powder as nutritionally equivalent to a complete meal. Nutrition.Fitness sells optional supplement products, so we have a commercial interest in this category. The calculation should remain the same whether you choose our product, another brand or ordinary food.

Pick two or three foods you enjoy, calculate their costs from your current labels and build meals around them. Browse the recipes for ways to use those ingredients. The winner is food you can afford, prepare and enjoy regularly.
shortAnswer: In our five-product Tesco comparison, dried lentils had the lowest ingredient cost per 25g of protein, followed by kidney beans, chickpeas, yogurt and chicken. The calculation uses each product’s stated dry, drained or raw weight. It is a comparison tool, not a recommended portion or a complete measure of nutrition; taste, variety, preparation and food waste also matter.

title: Is protein powder worth the money, or is food better value?
summary: Weigh up price, convenience and what is already in your meals.
bodyHtml:
Protein powder is worth considering when it solves a real problem: an awkward breakfast, limited food storage at work, or a convenient way to add protein to something you already enjoy. It is less useful when you buy it because you think getting fit requires a tub in the kitchen.

The fair comparison has two parts. What does a similar amount of protein cost? And what job does the purchase need to do? A shake can provide protein conveniently. A meal also needs to feed you.

Compare protein with protein, not scoops with portions

Pack prices can mislead because portions vary. Divide the delivered price by the total grams of protein in the pack, then multiply by 25. That gives you the cost of 25g of protein for comparison. The 25g figure is a shopping yardstick, not a personal intake recommendation.

Illustrative purchaseProtein in the whole packCost per 25g protein
£24 powder containing 800g protein800g£0.75
£2 food pack containing 50g protein50g£1.00
£4 food pack containing 125g protein125g£0.80

These are invented arithmetic examples, not supermarket prices or nutrition figures for named foods. Use the price and label on the product you are buying. Include delivery, and compare edible quantities consistently: drained tins, bones and raw-versus-cooked weights can otherwise make the figures unreliable.

As a real price snapshot checked on 15 September 2026, Myprotein's vanilla Impact Whey page displayed £31.99 for 900g and 30 servings. Its selected nutrition table listed 72g protein per 100g of powder. That is about £1.07 per 30g serving or £1.23 per 25g of labelled protein using the per-100g declaration, before delivery. The selected option was marked out of stock, so this is a published-price example, not a promise that you can buy it today.

Food is doing more than one job

Choosing everything by the cheapest protein number would produce a peculiar weekly menu. Beans might belong in tonight's chilli. Yoghurt might be breakfast. Eggs might become a quick meal when the fridge looks uninspiring. Buying those foods can replace food you would have bought anyway.

The government's Eatwell Guide describes a balanced diet across different food groups. Protein is part of that picture. A powder's protein figure does not tell you whether your overall meals offer enough variety.

Ask what the powder replaces. If it replaces a more expensive shake you already buy, the saving is easy to calculate. If you add it on top of meals that already work for you, it is an extra cost. If you start skipping lunch because a plain protein shake seems cheaper, you are comparing different things; ordinary protein powder is not automatically a complete meal replacement.

Convenience has value, but only when you use it

There is nothing wrong with paying a little more to make a busy day easier. Someone without a fridge at work faces different options from someone cooking at home. Someone who dislikes milky drinks may get better value from food even when the powder wins on paper.

Try a small pack or sample before a large order. A £20 purchase used completely can be better value than a £15 bargain that stays in the cupboard. Include the cost of milk, flavour additions and any shaker you actually need. You do not need to rebuild the kitchen around one drink.

When I would choose each option

  • Choose food first when you enjoy it, can store it and it fits meals you already eat.
  • Consider powder when a specific meal or snack is hard to organise and you like the product.
  • Choose a mixture when food works most days and a powder helps occasionally.
  • Buy neither extra food nor powder purely to hit an arbitrary number from an advert.

Check allergens on the exact flavour and formulation. A whey product comes from milk; a smaller lactose figure does not make it suitable for someone with a milk allergy. If you have a medical condition affecting your diet, ask your healthcare professional before deliberately increasing protein or adding supplements.

Our commercial interest, plainly

Nutrition.Fitness has a commercial interest in supplements. That does not make them necessary for using NUFI or starting a programme. Supplements and flavour shots are optional, separately priced purchases. If food does the job for less, that is a good outcome.

Start with three ordinary days of meals, without changing them. Identify whether there is an actual practical gap, then compare two ways to fill it. Our recipe collection can help with food ideas. The useful question is: which option would you willingly use next Tuesday, and what will it really cost?

title: Why are some protein powders so expensive? What you’re actually paying for
summary: Understand ingredients, processing, testing, pack sizes and branding.
bodyHtml:
Some expensive protein powders have a feature you may value: a different protein source, greater concentration, a particular certification or a format you prefer. Others cost more without giving you anything useful for your circumstances. The price tag cannot tell you which is which.

You are entitled to ask a seller why their product costs more. A clear answer should name the difference and show evidence. “Premium” printed in a large font is not that answer.

A real comparison of two displayed prices

On 15 September 2026, Myprotein displayed these prices and label values for selected vanilla products. Delivery is excluded. The concentrate selection was marked out of stock, so check availability as well as the current basket total.

Selected productDisplayed pack priceDeclared protein per 100g powderApproximate cost per 25g protein
Impact Whey, 900g£31.9972g£1.23
Impact Whey Isolate, 900g£39.9982g£1.35

The calculation uses each 900g bag and its per-100g protein declaration, giving a consistent basis across these guides. The isolate costs £8 more per bag, but around 12p more per equivalent 25g of protein. That does not establish which you should buy. It simply makes the price difference easier to judge. Flavours, promotions and label changes can alter the comparison.

What the higher price might buy

Protein concentration is one visible difference. The manufacturer describes additional filtration for isolate to reduce fat, lactose and sugar. This can matter to someone choosing a particular formulation. It does not mean everybody needs isolate, or that it guarantees more progress than a suitable cheaper option.

The same page says its isolate is not completely lactose-free. Both products contain milk. Do not treat a price premium or the word “isolate” as an allergy claim.

You may also be paying for flavour development, packaging, smaller production runs, retail distribution, advertising or brand recognition. Without a manufacturer's cost breakdown, nobody outside that business can honestly tell you what proportion of the price pays for each. A useful comparison focuses on the benefits you can verify rather than guessing the company's margins.

Testing is worth understanding properly

Testing claims need a name and scope. Informed Sport, for example, describes testing every certified product batch for banned substances before release and provides a searchable product and batch database. That is a specific process relevant to athletes concerned about prohibited substances.

It is not a promise of muscle gain, proof that you need a supplement, or the same thing as every other testing programme. Check the exact product and batch where applicable. A logo on one product does not certify every tub sold by the brand.

Ask what has been tested: banned substances, protein content, microbiological quality or something else? Ask who performed it and how you can verify the claim. The phrase “lab tested” without those details gives you little to compare.

Three ways a cheap-looking pack becomes expensive

  • A lower pack price hides a smaller quantity. Compare weights and protein concentration.
  • A tiny advertised serving makes the cost per serving look low. Compare equivalent protein amounts.
  • A large saving depends on buying several bags or joining a subscription. Compare the actual total commitment.

A “was” price is not your saving against every competing offer. The useful saving is the difference between what you would actually pay for two suitable options today. Add delivery before deciding, and avoid adding products you do not need merely to qualify for free shipping.

What I would ask before paying more

First, name the benefit: “I prefer this format”, “this exact product has the certification my sport requires”, or “this formulation suits my requirements”. Then ask whether a cheaper suitable option provides it too.

Second, test your preference where practical with a smaller pack. We have researched these labels; we have not tasted or mixed these products for this article. Taste reviews can suggest what to try, but your preference determines whether you use the purchase.

Third, set a realistic consumption pattern. If you only want powder occasionally, a larger pack may occupy money and cupboard space for months. Paying slightly more per serving for a smaller quantity can be the sensible decision.

When spending more is unlikely to help

If you cannot name the difference you want, pause. A more expensive shake cannot organise your week, teach exercise technique or make an unsuitable programme fit your life. Those may be the actual problems worth spending time or money on.

Nutrition.Fitness's interest in selling supplements should not decide your purchase. We should meet the same standard of clear ingredients, quantities and pricing we ask of other sellers. Compare any future product in our shop on that basis. If a less expensive alternative meets your needs, there is no prize for spending more.

title: How much does a basic home gym cost? Essentials for different budgets
summary: Work out what you need now, what can wait and how to compare equipment.
bodyHtml:
A basic home gym can begin with no new equipment. A clear space, suitable clothing you already own and an appropriate equipment-free routine may be enough to start. You can add a mat, bands or weights when your chosen exercises give you a reason to buy them.

You do not need a garage that looks like a sports centre. You need a setup you can use safely without a twenty-minute furniture removal operation before every workout.

Two actual prices to anchor your budget

On 15 September 2026, Decathlon displayed a set of three resistance bands at £17.99 and a 20kg cast-iron dumbbell set at £39.99. Those two products total £57.98 before any shipping. These are selected advertised products, not market averages or a claim that this combination suits every beginner.

A “20kg set” describes the combined set, not necessarily two 20kg dumbbells. Read the included plates, bars, collars and maximum loading before comparing it with another set. Band resistance labels also should not be read as identical to a fixed dumbbell load throughout an exercise.

Choose a spending level around a real routine

Budget approachWhat to considerWhat can wait
£0 in new equipmentExisting suitable space, clothing and equipment-free guidanceAll equipment until you identify a need
Illustrative £50 capOne priority item, with room for delivery or a mat if requiredA full matching set and decorative storage
Illustrative £150 capWeights suited to your programme, floor protection and storage as neededBench or machine without a planned use
Illustrative £500 capA more capable setup selected against space, loading and progression needsAnything chosen only because the budget allows it

The round budgets are spending scenarios, not complete retailer bundles or quotes. At any level, compare actual delivered prices before ordering. A mat may be useful; specialist flooring may be unnecessary for some activities and inadequate for others. The equipment and floor need to suit what you plan to do.

Buy for the next stage, not an imagined future

Choose your routine first. If it uses a pair of dumbbells, establish the starting loads, available increments and how exercises can progress. A very light fixed pair might become limiting quickly for some movements, while a heavy pair may be unusable for others.

Adjustable equipment can offer several loads in one footprint, but adjustment speed and storage matter. If changing plates will interrupt a short session, you may prefer a different arrangement. Product dimensions should include the space needed to move around it, not just the space it occupies in a catalogue photograph.

Free guidance is available. The NHS links to free home workout videos, including strength sessions. Paid equipment is not a prerequisite for seeing whether home exercise suits you. Choose a session appropriate to your current abilities rather than assuming every “beginner” video means the same thing.

Count the costs that are easy to miss

  • Delivery, assembly and getting heavy boxes upstairs.
  • Suitable floor protection and clearance around furniture.
  • Storage that keeps weights and bands away from children.
  • Replacement parts, compatible plates and the seller's returns process.
  • Instruction if you need help using equipment or choosing exercises.
  • An app or programme, if you decide one adds enough value.

Second-hand kit can reduce the purchase price, but inspect its condition. Missing collars, damaged bands, unstable benches and unclear weight limits are reasons to pause. Use anchors only as instructed by the manufacturer; ordinary doors and furniture are not automatically exercise equipment.

Compare the cost against use, without promising a payback

Suppose you spend an illustrative £150 and use the kit twice a week for 26 weeks. That is 52 sessions, or about £2.88 of equipment cost per session. If you use it ten times, the figure is £15. The equipment cost is the same; the usefulness differs.

That calculation leaves out replacement, instruction and any membership you retain. A home gym has not “paid for itself” merely because its price equals six months of gym fees. It only replaces that spend if you would otherwise have paid those fees and genuinely stop paying them.

When a gym or instructor may be better value

If you need varied heavy equipment, value a separate place to train or want supervision, a gym may suit you better. If home exercise fits around caring responsibilities and travel makes visits difficult, a compact home setup may be more useful even without a dramatic saving.

Start by checking the equipment requirements of a suitable programme. Then ask: what is the smallest purchase that lets me complete the next four weeks? Build from experience. The spare room does not need to become a showroom before you can begin.

title: What does a gym membership really cost? Joining fees, extras and cancellation terms
summary: Check the commitment as well as the headline monthly price.
bodyHtml:
The number on the gym advert is the starting point. Your real bill depends on the club, membership type, joining fee, extras and how long you are committed to paying. Travel and parking can change the comparison just as much as a difference in monthly fees.

The best value gym is one that offers the access and support you need at a total cost you can sustain. A bargain membership on the wrong side of town may be a bargain you rarely use.

What published prices tell you, and what they do not

Checked on 15 September 2026, PureGym's national membership page listed Off-peak from £17.99 per month, Core from £22.99 and Plus from £28.99, each plus a joining fee. Off-peak access times vary by gym; the page also distinguishes monthly options from memberships paid in advance.

Those are starting prices, not a quote for Leeds or any particular club. Select the location, access level and start date to see your actual offer. Read what is included there. Do the same with local leisure centres, independent gyms and other chains rather than assuming each provider packages services alike.

Use one total for a fair comparison

For the period you expect to train, add membership payments, joining fees and unavoidable extras. Then add your likely travel cost. Keep optional purchases separate so you can see which ones you genuinely want.

Illustrative first-year comparisonGym AGym B
Monthly fee, paid 12 times£25 × 12 = £300£30 × 12 = £360
Joining fee£20£0
Illustrative parking: 8 visits per month£2 × 96 = £192£0
Total across 12 months£512£360

These are invented examples, not quotes from named gyms. Gym A's lower headline fee still produces a higher total under these assumptions. If you walk there or parking is free, its total changes. Use your own circumstances, not the example's.

Check the billing unit too. A fee charged every four weeks is not the same as a calendar-month payment: a 52-week year contains 13 four-week periods. Twelve calendar-month payments contain 12 bills. Compare totals using the actual schedule rather than quietly treating both as “monthly”.

Which extras matter?

Check whether classes, swimming, inductions, lockers and access to another branch are included where you need them. Ask whether personal training is separately charged and whether a consultation is simply an introduction or includes an ongoing service. “Support available” does not tell you how much individual time you receive.

Ignore an upgrade's long feature list until you know which features you would use. A guest pass has value if a friend will join you. Earlier class booking has value if your preferred classes fill up. Free drinks are unlikely to rescue a membership whose opening times do not work for you.

Read the exit before joining

Before paying, find answers to four questions: what is the minimum commitment, how do I cancel, what is the notice deadline, and what happens to any money paid in advance? Save the terms and confirmation that apply to your own purchase.

For example, PureGym publishes a monthly cancellation guide as well as its broader membership terms. Use the instructions for the membership you actually buy. Do not assume a monthly payment automatically means a one-month commitment, or that stopping attendance ends payments.

If you want to pause for travel or other circumstances, ask about freeze charges, duration and what happens afterwards. A pause is useful only if the terms solve your situation. These are purchase checks, not a statement that every gym has the same rules.

Try your actual routine before choosing

Visit at the time you would normally train. Can you get there after work? Is the equipment you want available? Does the changing area work for you? Can you book the sessions you need? A quiet midday tour will not answer what a weekday evening feels like.

Use a day pass, tour or trial where one is available, checking its price and conditions. Do not assume a free trial exists. If childcare, confidence or lack of direction is the real barrier, discuss that directly; a cheaper membership alone may not address it.

When another option may be better

If you need no specialist equipment and home training fits your day, a suitable home programme may be enough. If you want technique feedback or individual support, some paid instruction may be more useful than an upgrade full of facilities. If you enjoy group sessions and attend reliably, a class-focused option may earn its cost.

NUFI's programme and meal-planning membership is a separate purchase from gym access. Count both if you intend to use both. Before choosing a programme, write down two realistic weekly training slots and the equipment it needs. Then price the places where you can actually complete it.

title: Does meal planning save money? A worked example for a busy household
summary: Compare planned shopping, leftovers and food waste across a normal week.
bodyHtml:
Meal planning can save money, but writing a menu is not what creates the saving. The saving comes from buying useful quantities, using what you already have and avoiding replacement purchases when dinner becomes inconvenient.

If your weekly plan requires three supermarkets, six new spices and an evening you do not have, it may increase the bill. A useful plan resembles your actual household, including the night everyone arrives home at different times.

A comparison that counts the same meals

The example below covers seven evening meals for a four-person household. It excludes breakfasts, lunches, snacks, drinks, toiletries and energy costs. These are invented figures to show the calculation, not a current supermarket basket or a claim about what your family should spend.

Illustrative evening-meal spendingLess organised weekPlanned week
Main shopping purchases allocated to dinners£55£50
Top-up purchases allocated to dinners£12£5
One replacement takeaway dinner£28£0
Total cash spent on those dinners£95£55
Estimated value of cupboard ingredients used£5£5
Total resources used or purchased£100£60

Both weeks feed the same four people on seven evenings. In the less organised week, the takeaway replaces a planned home dinner; it is not an eighth meal. Purchased dinner ingredients not eaten that week are assumed to be wasted in this example. If they remain safely available for a future meal, credit that stock rather than counting it as lost.

The difference is £40 under these assumptions. It is not a promised weekly saving. If your household already avoids waste and last-minute purchases, your saving could be much smaller or zero. If the planned week takes considerably more time or cooking energy, those costs belong in your decision too.

Turn the numbers into a workable week

Start with the diary. Put the quickest dinner on your busiest evening. Choose a few meals the household already eats, then reuse ingredients with a purpose: vegetables for a traybake and a pasta sauce, for example. There is no requirement for seven different dinners or seven days of identical boxes.

Plan a fallback meal that can wait in the freezer or cupboard. It is useful because plans change, not because buying takeaway is a moral failure. If a takeaway is something the family enjoys and can afford, include it deliberately in the budget instead of pretending it will never happen.

Check the fridge, freezer and cupboard before writing the shopping list. “Already paid for” does not mean free, but using it before buying more can reduce the cash you need this week. Keep a note of expensive ingredients used up so that next week's replenishment bill does not come as a surprise.

Watch the difference between portion cost and checkout cost

A recipe may use 20p worth of a spice, but if you do not own it you have to buy the whole jar. Four meals described as £2 per portion can still require a much larger first shop when each needs new cupboard ingredients.

For an honest budget, keep two figures: what you pay at the checkout and what the meals consume. Leftover rice, frozen vegetables and cupboard ingredients carry value into another week. Fresh ingredients without another planned use may not. Larger packs offer value only if you use them safely.

Plan leftovers safely

The Food Standards Agency advises cooling and refrigerating cooked leftovers within two hours and eating them within 48 hours, or freezing them if that will not be possible. Read its chilling and freezing guidance and follow any stricter instructions for specific foods. Do not build a plan around leaving a week's cooked meals in the fridge.

Label portions with the contents and date. Freeze planned later portions promptly rather than waiting until you are unsure whether they are still suitable. Buying less wastefully should never depend on guessing food safety.

Does paying for a planning tool make sense?

You can plan with paper, a notes app or a spreadsheet. Paid tools need to earn their cost through usefulness, convenience or support; the existence of a subscription does not prove it saves money.

For an illustrative tool costing £10 a month, saving £2 on each of four weekly shops produces £8, so grocery savings alone have not covered the fee. Saving £4 on each produces £16. You might still value saved time, but separate that preference from a claim of cash savings. Test your own receipts rather than extending one unusually expensive week into an annual prediction.

NUFI is designed around programmes and meal planning, with supplements optional. Its current site is a preview, so do not assume a working account or checkout from the example pages. Compare the listed membership prices with what you actually want help doing.

A useful first step costs nothing: choose four familiar dinners, one flexible leftover option and two easy fallback plans. Browse recipe ideas, make one list, then review what was eaten and spent. Keep the parts that made life easier.

title: Are supplement subscriptions cheaper? Discounts, delivery and commitments explained
summary: Compare the full recurring cost, renewal price and cancellation conditions.
bodyHtml:
A supplement subscription can reduce the price of something you already buy regularly. It can also create a steady supply of products you have stopped wanting. The discount is only useful when the product, quantity and schedule fit your actual use.

Compare the total you will pay over the same period, including any deliveries you are committed to receiving. “Save 20%” answers only one small part of the question.

Start with what you would buy anyway

Write down the exact product, pack size and how long a pack normally lasts. Then price that quantity as one-off purchases and as a subscription. Compare today's genuine one-off price, including any offer available to you, rather than assuming a crossed-out reference price is what you would otherwise pay.

Illustrative three-pack purchaseOne-off ordersSubscription
Product price per pack£30£24
Delivery per pack£4£0
Total for three packs£102£72

These are invented figures, not a retailer's current offer. If you genuinely need three packs, the subscription saves £30 under these assumptions. If you wanted only one pack and the subscription commits you to three, you spend £72 instead of £34. A lower unit price has produced a higher bill.

Buying three packs in a single one-off order may change the delivery calculation too. Use the purchasing pattern you would realistically choose on both sides.

Make delivery frequency match consumption

Consider an illustrative 30-serving pack used three times a week. It lasts ten weeks. Over 52 weeks, you use 156 servings, a little more than five packs. A delivery every calendar month sends 12 packs, or 360 servings, before any pauses.

At an illustrative £24 per pack, twelve deliveries cost £288. Six one-off packs at an illustrative delivered price of £34 cost £204 and provide 180 servings. Those are different quantities deliberately shown to illustrate over-ordering, not a claim that one-off prices are always better.

You might use the extra stock later, but your money is tied up and shelf life matters. Do not change how much you consume to keep up with deliveries. Change the schedule, skip where permitted or reconsider the subscription.

Read the exact offer

On 15 September 2026, Myprotein's UK subscription page described flexible general subscription features and separately displayed a named Cyber offer requiring three deliveries before pausing, skipping or cancelling. Its stated initial discounted price applied to those first three deliveries. This does not mean every subscription has that minimum.

The important lesson is to identify which offer your basket contains. When headline wording and a promotion's detailed conditions differ, ask for written clarification before paying. Save the offer and order confirmation so you can refer to the terms attached to your own purchase.

Seven questions worth answering first

  • What is the first payment, including delivery?
  • What will later deliveries cost, and is any price fixed?
  • How many orders am I committing to receive?
  • How often are orders dispatched, and when are payments taken?
  • Can I change flavour, quantity or frequency, and what is the deadline?
  • How do I pause or cancel, and when does that affect the next order?
  • What happens if the product is unavailable or a substitution is proposed?

A four-week delivery interval is also different from monthly delivery. Over 52 weeks, a four-week cycle contains 13 periods. Check the actual dispatch calendar, including the first order, instead of multiplying every recurring offer by twelve.

Put a reminder before any change deadline if you do subscribe. Revisit the arrangement when your routine changes; being busy, travelling or simply going off a flavour are normal reasons to need fewer deliveries.

Try the product before committing to more of it

Check ingredients and allergens, then try a suitable small quantity if available. Reviews cannot guarantee that you will enjoy a flavour or find it practical. We have not conducted a taste or mixability test for this article, so there is no sensory verdict hiding behind the price discussion.

Assess the whole bundle if a subscription includes several products. If you only want the powder, do not assign full value to extras you would never buy separately. An included shaker is useful if you need one; the fifth shaker does not have the same value.

Where Nutrition.Fitness fits

NUFI's core programme and meal-planning membership is separate from optional supplements and flavour shots. We do not quote a fixed Nutrition.Fitness supplement-subscription saving here because product prices, delivery schedules and final terms have not been verified for a live purchase.

Any offer shown in our shop should be judged using the same questions. Before paying for a bundle, ask for the membership cost, physical-product cost, delivery schedule and cancellation terms separately. That makes it easier to keep the parts you value and spot a commitment that does not suit you.

If you have not used a product before, or you use it only occasionally, a one-off purchase may be the more sensible start. A subscription should follow an established need, not create one.

title: What does a 12-week fitness programme cost, and what happens when it ends?
summary: Understand the initial fee, level of support and options after the programme.
bodyHtml:
A 12-week programme can be free, a one-off paid plan or part of a much more expensive coached service. The duration alone tells you very little about value. What matters is what you receive, what you can realistically use and what happens when the twelve weeks finish.

Before looking at a transformation photograph, look at the service description. Are you buying instructions, access to software, group support or a person's ongoing time? Those are different purchases.

Free is a real option

The NHS offers a free 12-week Weight Loss Plan app. It focuses on weight-management habits and tracking; it is not a substitute for individual exercise instruction or a tailored coaching service. Its existence is a useful reminder that a twelve-week format does not, by itself, justify a fee.

A weight-loss plan is not appropriate for everyone's goals or circumstances. If you have a medical condition, a prescribed diet or a current or past eating disorder, discuss changes with a healthcare professional. Becoming fitter does not require making weight loss your objective.

Work out what a paid plan actually includes

Type of purchaseWhat to verifyWhat should not be assumed
Self-guided written planExercises, progression, explanations and access periodPersonal replies or changes made for you
App membershipUsable features, programme options, support and renewalOne-to-one human coaching
Group programmeSession timetable, attendance requirements and group sizeUnlimited individual attention
Individual coachingWho coaches you, scheduled contact, reviews and scopeMedical care or guaranteed results

Ask to see an example week before buying. “Weekly support” might mean a recorded lesson, a group call or a personal review. Ask which, how long it lasts and how missed weeks are handled. If messages are included, ask who replies and the expected response time.

For a seller that quotes individually, request the written total rather than treating a price from somebody else's package as your quote. The right comparison is two services that solve the same problem.

The arithmetic should be easy to understand

Here are invented examples, not market averages or Nutrition.Fitness offers. A £120 plan costs £10 for each of its twelve programme weeks. A £480 coached package averages £40 per week. If the latter includes twelve individual reviews and the former includes none, price per week alone does not explain their difference.

Now include compulsory costs. If an illustrative £120 plan requires equipment costing £60, your starting spend is £180. If the plan also requires a separate £30 monthly gym membership for three billing months, that adds £90, bringing the example to £270. Check the dates: twelve weeks and three calendar months are not identical periods.

Do the same with food, supplements and app access. Ask which purchases are genuinely required and which are optional. If a programme cannot be followed without an additional purchase, that belongs in the total before you commit.

What NUFI's listed prices mean

NUFI's confirmed listed membership prices are £29.99 per month and £99 per year. The annual option is one £99 upfront payment, equivalent to £8.25 per month for comparison. Twelve monthly payments total £359.88. Three monthly payments total £89.97, but that is billing arithmetic, not a separately confirmed twelve-week offer.

NUFI is designed as the core programme and meal-planning system, with tracking and AI-coach features. Supplements and flavour shots are optional, separately charged products. These prices do not imply individual human-coaching hours or an all-inclusive physical-product bundle.

The current website is a preview, with payment and login not connected. Review the pricing page, and get the final live inclusions, renewal and cancellation terms before making any purchase. We have not confirmed a distinct twelve-week Nutrition.Fitness package, trial or refund promise.

Ask about week 13 before week 1

You should know whether access ends, continues free or renews for a fee. Ask whether you can keep the written plan, view your records and understand the next stage without buying an unexpected extension.

A worthwhile ending should leave you with practical decisions: which sessions you can maintain, how to adjust when a week gets busy and what progress you want to work on next. If there is an optional continuation service, its price and purpose should be clear before the initial plan ends.

Ask how the programme responds to a missed week, illness or a holiday. Repeating a week can be sensible; a rigid deadline should not pressure you to cram in sessions or restrict food to catch up. The calendar is an organisational tool, not a guarantee of a particular body by a particular date.

Choose the support that addresses your barrier

If you mainly need a structure and can follow it independently, a free or modestly priced plan may be enough. If confidence with equipment or individual adjustment is your main concern, qualified instruction may be the more useful spend. An app should not be presented as an equivalent to someone observing your technique.

Compare a suitable programme against your diary and available equipment. Then ask three questions: can I follow the first week, do I understand the entire cost, and do I know what happens at the end? Clear answers are more valuable than a dramatic promise.

title: Why am I not losing weight even though I’m eating better and exercising?
summary: Explore what to check when your effort and the scales seem to tell different stories.
bodyHtml:
You can put real effort into eating better and exercising and still see little movement on the scales. That does not make your effort imaginary. It means you need a clearer picture before deciding what to change.

The first question is whether weight loss is an appropriate goal for you. If it is, improved food quality alone does not guarantee it: total energy intake and expenditure still matter. The British Heart Foundation explains that food, activity, appetite, circumstances and medical factors can all complicate progress.

What exactly has not changed?

“Nothing is working” can mean a reading this morning, a month of similar readings or feeling disappointed with a photograph. Those are different questions. Write down what you expected to happen and over what period. If your expectation came from somebody else's transformation advert, it may need examining as carefully as your meal plan.

Also name the improvement you actually want. Getting upstairs more comfortably, learning to cook a few reliable meals and becoming stronger deserve their own attention. They are not consolation prizes handed out by an uncooperative bathroom scale.

Review a normal week without putting yourself on trial

A brief look at your routine can reveal practical obstacles. You do not have to weigh every ingredient or document your whole life. A few notes about meals, movement and difficult moments may be enough. If recording food makes you anxious or obsessive, leave that approach aside.

What you noticeA useful questionA practical experiment
Lunch is regularly missedIs the afternoon difficult because there is no meal available?Keep two lunches you genuinely like ready to assemble.
Your plan uses unfamiliar ingredientsAre you following it, or shopping for an imaginary version of your week?Rebuild one dinner around foods your household already buys.
Every workout requires a long journeyDoes the travel time make the routine impractical?Try a suitable home session on the busiest day.
You keep changing the programmeHave you given any approach a fair, consistent trial?Agree what you will assess and when, before buying another plan.

These are planning suggestions, not a diagnosis or a promise that one change will produce a particular weight result. Choose the obstacle that actually exists for you.

An example: solve the Tuesday problem

Imagine an adult who plans a cooked lunch and a gym visit every weekday. Tuesday involves back-to-back meetings and collecting children. Lunch becomes whatever is available; the gym closes before the evening settles down. Buying a more demanding programme does not remove either obstacle.

A useful revision could be a sandwich and fruit packed the night before, followed by a short suitable home workout on another day. The first test is whether the revised routine happens and leaves the person feeling adequately fed. Only then is it sensible to assess the longer-term outcome.

The NHS recommends making manageable changes and cautions against sudden dieting and skipping meals. “Try harder” is not a complete plan.

When more information is better than less food

If you have been consistent and remain concerned, a GP or registered dietitian can help you assess what is going on. Do not stop prescribed medication because an internet article suggests it might affect weight. Ask the prescriber. If food rules or weighing are affecting your wellbeing, prioritise support over further restriction.

Take useful context to an appointment: when the issue started, any symptoms, recent medication changes and what your routine looks like. You do not need a perfect spreadsheet to deserve help. The BHF guidance above also recommends discussing persistent difficulty with your GP.

Would paying for support solve the actual problem?

If you need convenient programme and meal-planning structure, that is the kind of role NUFI is being designed for. If you need someone to assess symptoms, supervise exercise technique or treat an eating difficulty, a general fitness app is not the equivalent service.

You can compare the NUFI prices and proposed membership, or start with free NHS resources and your existing food and exercise options. Before spending, finish this sentence: “I need help with…” A specific answer is more useful than “I need to be better”.
shortAnswer: Eating better and exercising can improve your routine without producing immediate weight loss. Start by checking the time period, the overall pattern of eating and what progress means to you. One scale reading cannot explain the cause. You may need a more workable plan, more time or individual support, rather than a stricter diet or another supplement.
