A sensible backup meal beats an ambitious recipe that never leaves the shopping list.

This is a research-based label and price comparison, not a taste test. We checked three Tesco listings on 15 September 2026 because they provided visible UK prices and nutrition panels. This small sample is not a ranking of every supermarket. Nutrition.Fitness has a commercial interest in meal planning and supplements; none of that makes a ready meal a failure.

Three options, with the figures kept in context

ProductListed single-pack priceProtein for the whole prepared packSalt for the whole prepared pack
Tesco Chicken Shawarma, 400g£3.7537.7g in detailed table; highlight says 34g1.63g
Tesco 3 Bean Chipotle Chilli, 400g£2.2519.2g1.37g
The Gym Kitchen Salt & Pepper Chicken, 400g£4.0029g1.4g

Prices are listed grocery prices in GBP, excluding delivery and any basket fees. Availability and checkout prices can vary. The bean chilli's panel uses a 358g cooked pack weight; the pack is sold as 400g. We have used whole-pack figures rather than multiplying a cooked figure by an uncooked weight.

The Shawarma protein figures conflict, so check the physical label. We will not declare a precise protein-value winner using unresolved information.

What can we reasonably conclude?

The bean chilli is the lowest single-pack price in this sample and is listed as vegan. The Gym Kitchen meal provides an option between the other two on published protein per pack. Shawarma has the highest displayed protein figure whichever of its conflicting numbers you use, but that does not automatically make it the best dinner.

There is also a loyalty offer on Shawarma: three eligible meals for £8, as displayed when checked. That averages about £2.67 per meal only when the purchase qualifies. You still spend £8 upfront. A multibuy is useful if all three get eaten; it is expensive fridge decoration if they do not.

Compare the whole dinner cost

Imagine you add a £1 side to a £3 main. Your dinner costs £4, not £3. This is illustrative arithmetic, not a price claim about these products. Apply the same principle to meals you make yourself: count the ingredients used, then account for the rest of the pack and whether it will be eaten.

Time matters as well. Someone coming home late may reasonably pay more for less preparation. Someone feeding four people may find a shared pan of chilli more convenient than heating four trays. Neither choice earns extra moral points.

Compare ready meals with the alternative you would actually choose that evening. If that is a purchased takeaway, use that price. If it is leftovers already in the freezer, acknowledge their cost too. Comparing against an imaginary homemade meal you never have time to cook produces an imaginary saving.

Our shopping checks

  • Use the whole-pack nutrition panel if you intend to eat the whole pack.
  • Check the ingredients and allergen information on the current pack, including any sauce.
  • Look at salt, fibre, vegetables and portion suitability alongside protein.
  • Decide whether you need an accompaniment to make a satisfying meal.
  • Check storage, use-by dates and whether it is suitable for freezing.
  • Buy one before committing to a large bundle when the flavour is unfamiliar.

For example, Tesco lists Shawarma as unsuitable for freezing, while the bean chilli is a frozen product. That makes a practical difference if you want an emergency meal available next month. The storage instructions linked above matter more than the word “protein” on the sleeve.

What we cannot tell you from a label

We have not tasted these meals, timed preparation or tested how filling they feel. We will not award stars for chicken texture or sauce flavour using somebody else's opinion. Treat retailer ratings as individual experiences, not a guarantee that you will enjoy the same thing.

Your next step is to pick one realistic backup meal and decide which busy evening it covers. Build it into a simple weekly plan alongside the meals you already cook. Our recipe ideas can help with the cooking nights; convenient food can take care of the others.

title: Budget protein powders: ingredients, labels and price compared
summary: A research-based comparison using a consistent scorecard and clearly explained testing.
bodyHtml:
The cheapest protein powder is not always the bag with the lowest price or the largest number of scoops. Compare the amount of protein you get for the delivered cost, then check ingredients and whether you will actually use it. Paying extra for a product you tolerate and enjoy can make sense. Paying extra because the tub looks serious is less persuasive.

This is a research-based label and price comparison, not hands-on testing. We checked official UK listings on 15 September 2026. We have not tested taste, mixability, digestive comfort or laboratory purity. Nutrition.Fitness plans to sell supplements, giving us a commercial interest. Our own products should face the same questions.

Three vanilla powders compared

Product and bagDisplayed offer priceProtein per 100g of powderCalculated cost per 25g of protein
Bulk Basic Whey, vanilla, 1.25kg£18.9959g£0.64
Bulk Pure Whey, vanilla, 1kg£31.9971g£1.13
Myprotein Impact Whey, vanilla, 900g£31.9972g£1.23

The selected Myprotein vanilla 900g option was marked out of stock when checked; its displayed price is a comparison example, not a currently purchasable offer. These calculations use displayed nutrition panels and the selected vanilla bags; confirm your own flavour and current label. Bulk's prices were visible in its UK product listings. All figures are GBP product prices before delivery, with offers as displayed on the check date. They are not a complete survey of the UK market or a promise that these offers remain available.

What does the calculation mean?

Take the bag weight in grams, multiply by protein per 100g divided by 100, and you have the labelled protein in the bag. Divide the price by that amount, then multiply by 25. This makes differently sized bags comparable without assuming every scoop contains the same amount of protein. We use the per-100g label values consistently; calculations using rounded per-serving declarations can give slightly different results.

The 25g figure is a comparison unit, not a personalised serving recommendation. For a purely illustrative example, a £20 bag containing 800g of protein works out at 62.5p per 25g. If delivery adds £4, it becomes 75p. Nothing about the powder changed; the actual cost did.

Bulk Basic's page displayed £3.95 standard delivery below £49. One £18.99 bag would therefore total £22.94 on that basis, or about 78p per 25g of labelled protein. Check postcode and checkout terms. Adding unwanted items to cross a free-delivery threshold can increase what you spend.

The ingredients explain an important difference

Bulk Basic contains both whey and soya protein. Bulk Pure Whey uses whey concentrate, and the selected Myprotein product also lists whey concentrate. All three contain milk; Basic also lists soya as an ingredient, while the other products have their own allergen details. The linked product panels are the source. Read the actual packet each time you buy.

A lower protein percentage is not automatically a bad product. In this sample, Basic still has the lowest calculated protein cost. Equally, if you specifically want whey without added soya protein, it is not interchangeable with the other two. Your requirement determines whether the difference matters.

For a vegan buyer these milk-based options are unsuitable. Someone who needs to avoid an allergen should rule out unsuitable products before comparing prices. A cheap product that does not meet your dietary requirements is not a bargain.

What about taste and mixability?

We cannot rank either without testing. Manufacturer descriptions such as creamy or smooth are claims, not our findings. Look for a small pack or sample when available and follow the mixing instructions. If you dislike it, buying a larger bag to reduce the price per scoop will only create a larger problem in the cupboard.

Decide how you intend to use it. Drinking with water, mixing into porridge and using in a recipe are different jobs. A powder that works for one may not suit another. Milk, yoghurt, fruit and flavour additions also change the total cost and nutrition; include them when comparing your usual shake.

When buying no powder is the better choice

First identify a real gap: perhaps a rushed breakfast or difficulty finding a convenient protein-containing snack. Then compare powder with food options you like, such as yoghurt, eggs, beans or tofu. If your normal meals already do the job, another subscription is optional.

Powder should not be sold as the admission ticket to getting fitter. The same applies to our planned supplement and flavour-shot range: those are optional physical products, separate from NUFI's programme and meal-planning membership. We are not claiming a live checkout on the current preview site.

Before choosing, write down your maximum delivered spend, ingredients you need to avoid and how you will use the product. Compare two suitable packs using the calculation above. If the real difficulty is organising meals, explore food ideas before filling the supplement shelf.
